A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PRISON, with matching framework, scenarios, main experiments, and appendices. Text extraction and rendered-page inspection provide sufficient access to the figures, tables, equations, and supplementary material for a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original simulations and evaluations of eight LLMs, including criminal-trait activation, detection accuracy, annotation validation, and persona experiments in Sections 4–5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds a human detection study, annotation-error analysis, scenario/context analyses, and evaluations of additional models.

M1.justification: The three-perspective PRISON procedure, five criminal traits, simulation and annotation prompts, information access, and judging agent remain unchanged. The additional model evaluations apply the existing framework.

E1.justification: The same 60 movie-derived scenarios, criminal-expression and detection tasks, and neutral topics are retained. Narrative outcomes and crime categories analyzed in v4 already appear in v3 Table 3. The human study samples 20 existing detection cases; it adds a comparator rather than new scenario or domain coverage.

E2.justification: v4 adds a human detection baseline in Appendix F.2.3, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B comparisons in Table 19, and DeepSeek-R1 against retained DeepSeek-V3 results in Table 20. These substantially extend the comparison set beyond the original eight LLMs.

E3.justification: The original five-turn, with/without Instruction settings remain unchanged. v4 introduces a controlled study with 100 participants and 20 sampled cases, qualification and attention checks, response-time exclusions, and majority-vote aggregation. It also introduces token-length grouping and additional model-size/context-capacity and reasoning comparisons.

E4.justification: v4 adds analysis of 100 agreed judge errors in Appendix D.2 and a human task-feasibility check in F.2.3. Appendix F.3 investigates narrative outcomes, crime types, safety-alignment behavior, input length, context capacity, and reasoning ability. These substantially expand checks of possible explanations for the expression–detection gap.

E5.justification: The existing Cohen’s kappa validation and Pearson correlation test are retained. New studies provide point estimates and descriptive token statistics without introducing repeated-run information, seeds, confidence intervals, or additional significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results in Tables 7–15 are retained. v4 adds reported human OTDA of 73.1% versus 42.5% for LLMs on the selected cases, scenario and context-length findings, and additional model results. Table 20 reports DeepSeek-R1 OTDA of 47.17% alongside the retained DeepSeek-V3 value of 43.62%.

T1.justification: The CTAR/OTDA definitions, logic-based trait formulations in Equations 3–7, and annotation-agreement derivation remain unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims: PRISON evaluates criminal potential and detection, criminal traits can emerge without direct instructions, and expression exceeds detection. The added appendix evidence supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: v4 interprets the human comparison as establishing sufficient Detective-perspective information and attributes model failures to social reasoning. Appendix F.3 argues against scenario design and context length as primary explanations, while discussing alignment and reasoning mechanisms. Appendix D.2 newly identifies concrete limitations of the GPT-4o judge.

D1.justification: Section 6 replaces the anonymous repository access link with a named GitHub repository link. Appendix F.2.3 documents the Credamo platform, participant eligibility, compensation, and quality controls. Existing simulation prompts, judging prompts, and default-inference disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v4 removes Ganguli et al. (2022), Karinshak et al. (2023), and Maras (2011) from the citations and bibliography. The broader positioning relative to ethical evaluation, social interaction research, and narrative simulation remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Language edits are localized to selected introductory and framework passages and author information. v4 adds acknowledgments and appendix subsections, updates cross-references, and renumbers the retained persona analysis from F.2.3 to F.2.4. The main narrative structure remains intact.

P2.justification: Tables 16–20 and Figure 8 add a substantial supplementary display set covering narrative/crime categories, token statistics, length-dependent performance, and model comparisons. Existing Figures 1–7 and Tables 1–15 are retained, with appendix reflow and added conference headers.

improvement.justification: The added judge-error analysis and human, scenario, and context comparisons improve transparency and provide useful validation absent from v3. Their force is limited: F.2.3 leaves unclear how majority voting over 20 items produces the reported 73.1% OTDA, and F.3.3 changes model size alongside claimed context capacity. These additions provide a limited net benefit, while some new interpretations exceed what the reported controls establish.
